scenarios.title: The overlapping acquisition
scenarios.situation: Contoso's hub VNet uses 10.0.0.0/16. An acquired company's VNet also uses 10.0.0.0/16, and both must peer with the hub.
choices: Re-address one side — peered VNets cannot have overlapping address spaces
Peer anyway; Azure resolves overlaps automatically
Use a VPN gateway instead of peering
Enable IP forwarding on all VMs
scenarios.why: VNet peering requires non-overlapping address spaces; Azure blocks peering creation when ranges overlap. Address planning (non-overlapping RFC 1918 space per VNet, room for growth) is the foundational design step — renumbering after the fact is painful.
scenarios.hint: Can two peered networks both claim 10.0.0.0/16?

scenarios.title: The gateway subnet
scenarios.situation: An admin tries to deploy a VPN gateway into a /29 subnet and the deployment fails.
choices: Gateway subnets need room for the gateway instances — Microsoft recommends /27 or larger (a /29 is too small)
The subnet needs an NSG first
scenarios.why: The gateway subnet hosts active/standby gateway instances plus platform addresses; Microsoft recommends /27 or larger. A /29 leaves no room after the 5 reserved addresses. Note: gateway subnets must be named exactly 'GatewaySubnet' and carry no NSG/UDR.
scenarios.hint: How much address room does a gateway subnet need, and what must it be named?

scenarios.title: The NVA inspection
scenarios.situation: All spoke-to-spoke and spoke-to-internet traffic must be inspected by a firewall NVA in the hub.
scenarios.prompt: How is traffic forced through the hub?
choices: User-defined routes (UDRs) in each spoke with 0.0.0.0/0 pointing to the hub NVA/firewall
VNet peering alone — it forces transit automatically
scenarios.why: Peering connects spokes to the hub but doesn't route spoke-to-spoke through it (non-transitive). UDRs with a default route to the hub firewall/NVA override system routes and force inspection — the classic forced-tunneling/hub inspection design.
scenarios.hint: Peering connects; what steers the packets through the firewall?

scenarios.title: The SNAT exhaustion
scenarios.situation: A spoke with 500 VMs behind a standard load balancer sees intermittent outbound connection failures under load.
scenarios.prompt: What is the likely cause and fix?
choices: SNAT port exhaustion — attach Azure NAT Gateway to the subnet for scalable outbound connectivity
The VMs need public IPs each
scenarios.why: Outbound SNAT ports are finite per public IP; hundreds of VMs sharing a few ports exhaust them. NAT Gateway provides up to 64k SNAT ports per public IP (up to 16 IPs) at the subnet level — the designed fix for large-scale outbound.
scenarios.hint: Hundreds of VMs sharing few outbound ports — what runs out, and what scales it?

scenarios.title: The Private Link name
scenarios.situation: After creating a private endpoint for a storage account, apps resolve the public name to the public IP instead of the private IP.
choices: A private DNS zone (privatelink.blob.core.windows.net) linked to the VNet with the correct A record
scenarios.why: Private endpoints need private DNS resolution: the privatelink.* zone linked to the VNet maps the service's public FQDN to the private endpoint IP. Without it, clients resolve the public IP and traffic leaves the VNet — silently defeating the purpose.
scenarios.hint: The endpoint exists but names still resolve publicly. Which DNS piece completes Private Link?

scenarios.title: The spreadsheet chaos
scenarios.situation: Five teams allocate VNet address space from a shared spreadsheet; overlaps and exhaustion keep happening.
scenarios.prompt: What brings order to IP address management?
choices: Azure IPAM / Virtual Network Manager with centrally planned pools and verification
scenarios.why: IP address management (IPAM) — planning non-overlapping pools per region/environment, reserving growth space, and verifying before deployment — prevents the overlap/exhaustion cycle. Azure Virtual Network Manager can centrally manage connectivity and security configs across VNets.
scenarios.hint: What's the process fix for spreadsheet-driven address chaos?

scenarios.title: The branch office link
scenarios.situation: A branch office with a static public IP needs its LAN to reach Azure VNets over an encrypted tunnel.
choices: Site-to-site VPN — IPsec tunnel between the on-premises VPN device and the Azure VPN gateway
scenarios.why: Site-to-site VPN connects entire on-premises networks to Azure via IPsec from the site's VPN device. Point-to-site is per-client; ExpressRoute is dedicated private connectivity (overkill for one small branch); peering is Azure-to-Azure only.
scenarios.hint: Whole branch LAN to Azure, encrypted — which VPN type?

scenarios.title: The remote admins
scenarios.situation: Twenty remote admins need encrypted access to Azure VNets from their laptops — no site VPN device involved.
choices: Point-to-site VPN — per-client VPN to the Azure VPN gateway
scenarios.why: Point-to-site VPN gives individual clients (laptops) an encrypted tunnel to the VNet via the VPN gateway — no on-premises VPN hardware needed. It's the remote-admin answer; site-to-site needs a site device.
scenarios.hint: Individual laptops, no site hardware — which VPN type?

scenarios.title: The replication pipe
scenarios.situation: A hospital replicates 8 TB nightly to Azure and needs consistent throughput, private connectivity, and an SLA.
choices: ExpressRoute — private dedicated circuit with predictable bandwidth and SLA
scenarios.why: ExpressRoute provides private, dedicated bandwidth (up to 100 Gbps) with SLA-backed latency/throughput — the choice for bulk, compliance-sensitive, or latency-sensitive traffic. VPN over the internet can't guarantee throughput.
scenarios.hint: Bulk nightly replication needing guaranteed private throughput — which circuit?

scenarios.title: The thirty branches
scenarios.situation: A retailer has 30 branches, each needing connectivity to Azure and to each other, managed centrally.
scenarios.prompt: What simplifies this hub-and-spoke at scale?
choices: Azure Virtual WAN — managed hub with integrated VPN/ExpressRoute/P2S and branch-to-branch transit
30 separate site-to-site VPNs with manual routing
scenarios.why: Virtual WAN provides a Microsoft-managed hub (vpn/ER/P2S gateways built in) with any-to-any branch connectivity and centralized routing/security policy — far simpler than meshing 30 site VPNs manually.
scenarios.hint: Thirty sites needing any-to-any through Azure — which managed hub?

scenarios.title: The two clouds
scenarios.situation: A company has ExpressRoute to Azure and a private connection to another cloud, and needs the two environments to talk privately via the providers' networks.
choices: ExpressRoute Global Reach — links two ExpressRoute circuits through Microsoft's network
A site-to-site VPN over the internet
scenarios.why: Global Reach connects ExpressRoute circuits together over Microsoft's backbone — e.g., Azure to another cloud's private interconnect — without traversing the public internet. It's circuit-to-circuit, not VNet peering.
scenarios.hint: Two private circuits needing to meet privately — which feature links circuits?

scenarios.title: The Office 365 path
scenarios.situation: An admin enables Microsoft peering on ExpressRoute expecting all Azure VNet traffic to use it.
choices: Microsoft peering is for Microsoft 365/Dynamics and public services; VNet traffic uses private peering
scenarios.why: ExpressRoute has two peering types: private peering (RFC 1918 traffic to your VNets) and Microsoft peering (public Microsoft services like M365). Enabling Microsoft peering doesn't route VNet traffic — that's private peering's job.
scenarios.hint: Which peering type carries traffic to your VNets versus to M365?

scenarios.title: The default internet path
scenarios.situation: A VM in a VNet reaches the internet directly. The admin wants all outbound traffic inspected by the hub firewall instead.
choices: A UDR with 0.0.0.0/0 pointing to the firewall's private IP — it overrides the system default route
An NSG rule — NSGs filter but don't route
A route table without any routes
scenarios.why: Azure system routes send internet-bound traffic directly out; a UDR default route (0.0.0.0/0 → firewall/NVA) overrides it — forced tunneling. NSGs filter traffic but never change its path; routing and filtering are separate mechanisms.
scenarios.hint: What overrides a system route to steer traffic elsewhere?

scenarios.title: The asymmetric routing
scenarios.situation: With a VPN gateway and ExpressRoute both connected, return traffic sometimes takes a different path than outbound, breaking stateful inspection.
scenarios.prompt: What routing feature fixes path consistency?
choices: BGP — dynamic routing lets both sides agree on best paths and fail over consistently
scenarios.why: BGP exchanges routes dynamically between on-premises and Azure, enabling consistent path selection and automatic failover across redundant connections. Static routes can't adapt, causing asymmetric paths that break stateful firewalls.
scenarios.hint: What makes both sides agree on routes dynamically?

scenarios.title: The overlapping routes
scenarios.situation: A route table has 10.0.0.0/16 → firewall and 10.0.1.0/24 → VNet peering. A packet for 10.0.1.50 arrives.
choices: 10.0.1.0/24 — longest prefix match wins over the broader /16
The system route wins over UDRs
scenarios.why: Longest prefix match: the most specific matching route wins, regardless of creation order. UDRs override system routes of equal specificity; among UDRs, specificity decides.
scenarios.hint: Two routes match. Which selection rule decides?

scenarios.title: The single firewall
scenarios.situation: All spoke traffic routes through one firewall NVA. During its maintenance, all outbound traffic stops.
scenarios.prompt: What design removes this single point of failure?
choices: An NVA cluster / Azure Firewall with availability zones — redundant inspection path
scenarios.why: Forced tunneling concentrates traffic on the inspection point, so it must be highly available: Azure Firewall is zone-redundant by default; third-party NVAs need active-active clustering behind a load balancer. Redundancy at the choke point is non-negotiable.
scenarios.hint: The choke point must not be a single VM. What makes inspection highly available?

scenarios.title: The storage detour
scenarios.situation: After enabling a service endpoint for Storage on a subnet, traffic to the storage account still hairpins through the hub firewall.
choices: Service endpoints inject a system route that takes precedence appropriately — check whether a UDR 0.0.0.0/0 is forcing it; service endpoint routes are more specific and should win for the service prefixes
Service endpoints don't work with UDRs at all
scenarios.why: Service endpoints add system routes for the service's public prefixes, which are more specific than a 0.0.0.0/0 UDR — so service traffic should bypass the firewall. If it doesn't, verify the endpoint is enabled on the right subnet and the storage firewall allows the VNet.
scenarios.hint: Which route should win for service traffic, and what would break it?

scenarios.title: The effective routes tool
scenarios.situation: An admin can't tell which of three route tables actually applies to a VM's NIC.
scenarios.prompt: What shows the final computed routes?
choices: Network Watcher's 'effective routes' view for the NIC — subnet + NIC route tables merged with system routes
scenarios.why: Effective routes (portal or Get-AzEffectiveRouteTable) shows the merged result: NIC route table + subnet route table + system routes, with the winning route per prefix. It's the authoritative answer to 'where will this packet go?'
scenarios.hint: Which view shows the merged, final routing decision for a NIC?

scenarios.title: The compliance mandate
scenarios.situation: Regulators require that database traffic never traverse a public endpoint — not even with IP restrictions.
scenarios.prompt: Which option truly removes the public endpoint from the path?
choices: Private endpoint — traffic goes to a private IP in the VNet; the public endpoint can be disabled
Service endpoint — keeps the public endpoint, only extends VNet identity
A VPN to the database's public IP
scenarios.why: Only private endpoints move traffic to a private IP inside the VNet and allow disabling public access entirely. Service endpoints keep the service's public endpoint (traffic stays on the backbone but the endpoint is still public) — insufficient for this mandate.
scenarios.hint: Which option eliminates the public endpoint rather than just restricting it?

scenarios.title: The partner service
scenarios.situation: A company wants to expose an internal API to a partner's VNet privately — without either side peering VNets or exposing public IPs.
choices: Private Link Service — publishes the internal load balancer as a private-link service the partner consumes via their own private endpoint
A public load balancer with IP whitelist
A site-to-site VPN to the partner
scenarios.why: Private Link Service (the provider side of Private Link) exposes your internal standard load balancer to consumers who create private endpoints in their own VNets — private connectivity with no peering, no public IPs, and consumer-driven approval.
scenarios.hint: How do you offer a private service to another tenant's VNet without peering?

scenarios.title: The partner's DNS
scenarios.situation: The partner's private endpoint resolves the service name to a public IP from their VNet.
scenarios.prompt: What's missing on the consumer side?
choices: Their own private DNS zone linked to their VNet mapping the service FQDN to the private endpoint IP
A change on the provider side
scenarios.why: Each consumer VNet needs its own private DNS zone linked locally — DNS resolution is per-VNet. The provider can't fix the consumer's resolution; the consumer links the privatelink zone (or a custom zone) to their VNet.
scenarios.hint: Whose DNS must map the name to the private IP?

scenarios.title: The internal app gateway
scenarios.situation: An application gateway must serve an internal HR app with no public exposure at all.
choices: Application Gateway with a private frontend IP only (no public frontend)
Application Gateway always requires a public IP
Put the gateway in the gateway subnet
scenarios.why: Application Gateway supports private-only frontend IPs for internal apps (WAF still available). It needs its own dedicated subnet — not the gateway subnet, which is reserved for VPN/ExpressRoute gateways.
scenarios.hint: Can an app gateway be fully private, and where does it live?

scenarios.title: The jump box replacement
scenarios.situation: The network team wants admins to reach VMs without public IPs, without a VPN client, and without managing jump boxes.
choices: Azure Bastion in the hub VNet (dedicated AzureBastionSubnet /26+) peered to spokes
An NVA jump box per spoke
scenarios.why: Bastion deployed once in the hub (in its own AzureBastionSubnet, /26 or larger) serves peered spokes — no public IPs on VMs, no VPN clients, no jump boxes to patch. It's the hub-and-spoke admin access pattern.
scenarios.hint: One deployment serving all peered spokes, no jump boxes — which service and subnet?

scenarios.title: The storage transit
scenarios.situation: A security review requires that all storage account traffic use encrypted transit and private networking.
scenarios.prompt: Which two settings combine to meet this?
choices: 'Secure transfer required' (HTTPS-only) plus private endpoints with public access disabled
HTTPS-only alone — still a public endpoint
Private endpoints alone — still allows HTTP
scenarios.why: Secure transfer required enforces HTTPS (encryption in transit); private endpoints with public network access disabled enforce private paths. Compliance needs both axes: encrypted AND private.
scenarios.hint: Which setting encrypts transit and which privatizes the path?

scenarios.title: The flaky branch link
scenarios.situation: A branch reports intermittent slowness to Azure. The team needs continuous latency/loss measurement, not a one-time test.
choices: Connection Monitor — synthetic tests on a schedule with latency, loss, and topology insights
NSG flow logs — show allowed/denied, not latency
scenarios.why: Connection Monitor runs scheduled synthetic probes between endpoints and tracks latency, packet loss, and hop topology over time — the tool for intermittent issues that one-time tests miss.
scenarios.hint: Which tool watches path health continuously over time?

scenarios.title: The denied traffic mystery
scenarios.situation: An app fails intermittently. The team suspects an NSG is dropping traffic but can't prove which rule.
choices: NSG flow logs (via Traffic Analytics) — 5-tuple flows with allow/deny decisions
Connection Monitor — measures latency, not rule decisions
Packet capture on the VM — sees packets, not NSG verdicts
scenarios.why: NSG flow logs record every flow's allow/deny verdict per rule through the NSG, stored in Log Analytics via Traffic Analytics for KQL querying. It's the authoritative record of what the NSG did.
scenarios.hint: Which log records the NSG's allow/deny verdict per flow?

scenarios.title: The malformed handshake
scenarios.situation: TLS handshakes to a backend fail. The team needs the actual packets to see what's malformed.
scenarios.prompt: Which Network Watcher tool captures them?
choices: Packet capture — captures VM NIC traffic to a storage account for Wireshark analysis
IP flow verify — simulates, doesn't capture
Connection troubleshoot — end-to-end check, no packets
scenarios.why: Network Watcher packet capture records real packets from a VM (or gateway) to blob storage for deep protocol analysis. It's the escalation when flow logs and verifiers can't explain the failure.
scenarios.hint: You need the actual bytes on the wire. Which tool captures them?

scenarios.title: The top talkers
scenarios.situation: The CISO asks: which external IPs talk most to our VNets, and are any data transfers suspiciously large?
scenarios.prompt: What answers this from flow data?
choices: Traffic Analytics — aggregates NSG flow logs into top talkers, geo distribution, and traffic patterns
scenarios.why: Traffic Analytics processes raw NSG flow logs into visual insights: top talkers, application ports, data-center/DC traffic distribution, and malicious-flow flagging — the analysis layer over flow logs.
scenarios.hint: Which layer turns raw flow logs into 'top talkers' insights?

scenarios.title: The undocumented estate
scenarios.situation: A new engineer inherits 40 VNets with unknown peering and gateway relationships.
choices: Network Watcher topology view — VNets, peerings, gateways, and connections mapped
scenarios.why: Network Watcher's topology generates a map of VNets, subnets, peerings, gateways, and NICs — the fastest way to comprehend an undocumented estate before making changes.
scenarios.hint: Which view draws the map of VNets, peerings, and gateways?

scenarios.title: The down tunnel
scenarios.situation: A site-to-site VPN tunnel is down. The on-premises team insists their device is fine.
scenarios.prompt: What is the systematic triage order?
choices: Check gateway health and connection status in Azure → verify shared key/IPsec parameters match → review gateway diagnostics and IKE logs
Delete and recreate the gateway immediately
scenarios.why: Triage VPN methodically: Azure connection status and gateway health first, then the usual culprits — mismatched pre-shared key, IKE/IPsec proposal mismatch, or NAT-T issues — using gateway diagnostics. Recreating the gateway is a last resort, not a first step.
scenarios.hint: What's the ordered triage for a down IPsec tunnel?

scenarios.title: The egress control
scenarios.situation: Compliance requires all internet-bound traffic from workloads to be filtered by FQDN (only approved domains) with TLS inspection.
choices: Azure Firewall Premium — FQDN filtering in network rules plus TLS inspection
NSG — filters by IP/port, not FQDN, no TLS inspection
Azure Firewall Basic — no TLS inspection
scenarios.why: Only Azure Firewall Premium offers TLS inspection; Standard and Premium both do FQDN-based filtering in network rules (layer 7 awareness NSGs lack). The tier choice hinges on the TLS inspection requirement.
scenarios.hint: FQDN filtering plus TLS inspection — which tier has both?

scenarios.title: The fifty firewalls
scenarios.situation: An enterprise runs many Azure Firewalls and needs one place to define rule collections inherited by all of them.
choices: Azure Firewall Manager with firewall policies — hierarchical rule inheritance across firewalls and Virtual WAN hubs
scenarios.why: Firewall Manager with Azure Firewall Policies lets you define rule collections once (including hierarchical base + local policies) and assign them across firewalls and secured virtual hubs — centralized governance for distributed enforcement.
scenarios.hint: What provides one policy definition inherited by many firewalls?

scenarios.title: The SQL injection attempt
scenarios.situation: A web app faces automated SQL injection and XSS probes. The team wants managed rule sets blocking OWASP Top 10 patterns at the edge.
choices: WAF on Application Gateway (regional) or Azure Front Door (global) with managed OWASP rule sets
Azure Firewall alone — L3/L4 + FQDN, not HTTP WAF rules
scenarios.why: Web Application Firewall (on App Gateway for regional, Front Door for global) inspects HTTP/S payloads against managed rule sets (OWASP CRS) blocking injection and XSS. Azure Firewall filters network traffic but isn't an HTTP WAF.
scenarios.hint: Blocking SQLi/XSS in HTTP payloads at the edge — which service?

scenarios.title: The gaming launch
scenarios.situation: A multiplayer game backend with public IPs expects volumetric DDoS attacks at launch and needs adaptive mitigation plus cost protection.
choices: DDoS Network Protection on the VNet — adaptive tuning, attack analytics, and cost protection for scaled-out resources
Basic (automatic) protection alone — no tuning or cost protection
scenarios.why: DDoS Network Protection (paid tier) adds adaptive per-app tuning, detailed attack telemetry, and cost protection against scale-out billing during attacks — beyond the always-on basic mitigation every VNet gets.
scenarios.hint: Adaptive tuning plus cost protection during an attack — which tier?

scenarios.title: The three-tier rules
scenarios.situation: A three-tier app (web/app/db subnets) needs: internet → web on 443 only; web → app on 8080; app → db on 1433; nothing else between tiers.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct NSG approach?
choices: Subnet-level NSGs with explicit allow rules per tier flow plus default deny — least-privilege segmentation
One NSG allowing everything between subnets
NIC-level NSGs only on the web tier
No NSGs; rely on the firewall alone
scenarios.why: Subnet-level NSGs implementing explicit allow rules for required tier-to-tier flows (with the default deny-all doing the rest) is textbook micro-segmentation. Each tier's NSG encodes exactly the flows that tier needs — nothing more.
scenarios.hint: How do NSGs enforce least-privilege between tiers?

scenarios.title: The DNS exfiltration
scenarios.situation: A security review worries that compromised VMs could use DNS tunneling to exfiltrate data past the firewall.
scenarios.prompt: What mitigates DNS-based exfiltration in the design?
choices: Azure Firewall DNS proxy with FQDN filtering + monitoring/alerting on anomalous DNS — DNS can't be simply blocked without breaking resolution
scenarios.why: DNS is essential, so the answer isn't blocking it: route DNS through the firewall's DNS proxy for FQDN policy enforcement and alert on anomalous query volumes/patterns (Defender for Cloud also flags DNS anomalies). Design acknowledges DNS as a control point, not just plumbing.
scenarios.hint: You can't block DNS outright. How do you control and watch it?

lessons.title: VNet Design — Core concepts
concepts: Address planning (non-overlapping RFC 1918 space per VNet, room for growth) is the foundational design step — renumbering after the fact is painful. IP address management (IPAM) — planning non-overlapping pools per region/environment, reserving growth space, and verifying before deployment — prevents the overlap/exhaustion cycle.

Peering prerequisites: vNet peering requires non-overlapping address spaces; Azure blocks peering creation when ranges overlap. Peering connects spokes to the hub but doesn't route spoke-to-spoke through it (non-transitive).

Gateway subnet: the gateway subnet hosts active/standby gateway instances plus platform addresses; Microsoft recommends /27 or larger. NAT Gateway provides up to 64k SNAT ports per public IP (up to 16 IPs) at the subnet level — the designed fix for large-scale outbound.

UDR: note: gateway subnets must be named exactly 'GatewaySubnet' and carry no NSG/UDR. UDRs with a default route to the hub firewall/NVA override system routes and force inspection — the classic forced-tunneling/hub inspection design.

example.walkthrough: Private endpoints need private DNS resolution: the privatelink.* zone linked to the VNet maps the service's public FQDN to the private endpoint IP. Without it, clients resolve the public IP and traffic leaves the VNet — silently defeating the purpose.

pitfalls: Common trap: use a VPN gateway instead of peering.
Common trap: the subnet needs an NSG first.
Common trap: an NSG rule allowing DNS.
Common trap: peer anyway; Azure resolves overlaps automatically.

lessons.title: Connectivity — Core concepts
concepts: Site-to-site VPN connects entire on-premises networks to Azure via IPsec from the site's VPN device. Point-to-site VPN gives individual clients (laptops) an encrypted tunnel to the VNet via the VPN gateway — no on-premises VPN hardware needed.
Hybrid connectivity: point-to-site is per-client; ExpressRoute is dedicated private connectivity (overkill for one small branch); peering is Azure-to-Azure only.
Point-to-site VPN: VPN over the internet can't guarantee throughput.

ExpressRoute: global Reach connects ExpressRoute circuits together over Microsoft's backbone — e.g., Azure to another cloud's private interconnect — without traversing the public internet. ExpressRoute has two peering types: private peering (RFC 1918 traffic to your VNets) and Microsoft peering (public Microsoft services like M365).

Dedicated connectivity: expressRoute provides private, dedicated bandwidth (up to 100 Gbps) with SLA-backed latency/throughput — the choice for bulk, compliance-sensitive, or latency-sensitive traffic.

Azure system routes send internet-bound traffic directly out; a UDR default route (0.0.0.0/0 → firewall/NVA) overrides it — forced tunneling.

Route override: longest prefix match: the most specific matching route wins, regardless of creation order. Effective routes (portal or Get-AzEffectiveRouteTable) shows the merged result: NIC route table + subnet route table + system routes, with the winning route per prefix.
BGP exchanges routes dynamically between on-premises and Azure, enabling consistent path selection and automatic failover across redundant connections.
Dynamic routing: nSGs filter traffic but never change its path; routing and filtering are separate mechanisms.

Compliance needs both axes: encrypted AND private.

Private Link Service: secure transfer required enforces HTTPS (encryption in transit); private endpoints with public network access disabled enforce private paths. OWASP protection: dDoS Network Protection (paid tier) adds adaptive per-app tuning, detailed attack telemetry, and cost protection against scale-out billing during attacks — beyond the always-on basic mitigation every VNet gets.

lessons.title: Azure Network Engineer — Core concepts
concepts: VNet peering is non-transitive and low-latency: it connects exactly two VNets. Spoke-to-spoke via a hub needs gateway-transit settings, forwarded-traffic allowance, and UDRs pointing at the hub appliance.

Hybrid links differ in kind: site-to-site VPN runs over the public internet with per-SKU throughput ceilings; ExpressRoute is a private circuit with predictable latency. They can coexist, with BGP controlling which path each side prefers.
Azure DNS has two faces: public zones for internet names, private zones for VNet-internal resolution — and a private zone only resolves in VNets explicitly linked to it, peering notwithstanding.

Load balancing is chosen by layer and scope: Load Balancer (L4, regional), Application Gateway (L7, regional, WAF, path routing), Front Door (L7, global), Traffic Manager (DNS-based steering, no proxying).

Network Watcher is the diagnostic toolkit: NSG flow logs show allow/deny verdicts per flow, Traffic Analytics aggregates them, Connection Troubleshoot tests a path hop by hop, and IP flow verify checks a specific packet against NSG rules.
User-defined routes override Azure's default system routes; a 0.0.0.0/0 route to a firewall (forced tunneling) makes the appliance a choke point that must explicitly allow the traffic.

example.code:
az network watcher test-connectivity --resource-group rg-net \
  --source-resource vm-app --dest-resource vm-db --dest-port 5432
az network watcher show-topology --resource-group rg-net --location eastus -o table
example.walkthrough: Test connectivity from one VM to another on a specific port — Network Watcher reports each hop and where the packet is dropped. The topology view maps the VNet, peerings, and appliances so you can see the path the test took.

pitfalls: Common trap: expecting peered spokes to reach each other through the hub with no transit configuration.
Common trap: forgetting the private DNS zone link on the second VNet and blaming peering for NXDOMAIN.
Common trap: sizing a VPN gateway for today's traffic and hitting the SKU throughput ceiling after growth.
Common trap: using Traffic Manager where you need TLS termination or path routing — it only answers DNS.

simulations.title: No route to the spoke
simulations.brief: A VM in the spoke VNet cannot reach the hub firewall. Peering shows 'Connected'. Work the evidence.

steps.symptom: Spoke-to-hub traffic fails despite peering status Connected.
options: Check the route tables and whether 'use remote gateways' / gateway transit is configured on the peering
Delete and recreate the peering — it must be corrupt
The VNet is too small — expand the address space
Reboot the VM — networking stacks get stuck
steps.explain: 'Connected' peering without gateway transit or correct routes is the classic hub-spoke failure: peering is up, but traffic has no route or no gateway to use. Check peering options and UDRs before rebuilding anything.

steps.symptom: The peering lacks gateway transit and the spoke has no route to the hub firewall.
options: Enable gateway transit on the peering and add the UDR pointing 0.0.0.0/0 at the hub firewall
Assign public IPs to all spoke VMs so they route directly
Move the firewall into the spoke VNet
Disable the firewall — it is blocking legitimate traffic
steps.explain: Hub-spoke routing is explicit: gateway transit on the peering plus user-defined routes steering traffic through the hub appliance. Public IPs or moving the firewall dodge the architecture.

simulations.debrief: You diagnosed hub-spoke routing at the right layer: peering state, then transit options, then routes. Connectivity is designed, not assumed.

simulations.title: The route table that hijacked traffic
simulations.brief: After a route-table change, the app subnet lost internet access. Review the routes and click the offending lines.

issues.description: The default route points at the firewall, but the firewall is down for maintenance — all outbound traffic blackholes.
issues.fix: During firewall maintenance, either fail the default route over or schedule the change in a window; never leave a dead next hop.

issues.description: Two default routes (lines 2 and 3) — Azure uses longest-prefix match, and identical 0.0.0.0/0 routes are ambiguous.
issues.fix: Keep exactly one default route; remove the duplicate so the intended path is deterministic.

simulations.debrief: You caught the routing sins: a dead next hop and duplicate default routes. Route tables are read top-to-specific — ambiguity is an outage waiting.

simulations.title: Peer or VPN?
simulations.brief: Two VNets need to talk. The junior engineer proposes a VPN gateway between them. Steer the design.

steps.text: Both VNets are in Azure, same tenant, non-overlapping address spaces. VPN gateway between them?

choices.label: Yes — VPN gateways connect networks
choices.feedback: A VPN gateway between two Azure VNets is cost and complexity for no reason when peering exists.

choices.label: No — VNet peering is the native, low-latency answer
choices.feedback: Correct — peering keeps traffic on the Azure backbone with no gateway hops.

steps.text: The gateway would cost ~$140/month and add latency. Reconsider:
Now the second VNet is in a different tenant (partner company). Still peering?

choices.label: Yes — cross-tenant peering works with consent
choices.feedback: Correct — VNet peering supports cross-tenant with proper authorization. The constraint changed, the answer adapted.

choices.label: No — tenants can never connect
choices.feedback: Wrong — cross-tenant peering is supported. Never let a false constraint kill a valid design.

simulations.debrief: You chose the right interconnect per constraint: peering for Azure-to-Azure, and you knew peering crosses tenants too. Design follows constraints, not habits.

sections.heading: VNet Design
items: Address — Address planning (non-overlapping RFC 1918 space per VNet, room for growth) is the foundational design step — renumbering after the fact is painful. IP address management (IPAM) — planning non-overlapping pools per region/environment, reserving growth space…

Peering prerequisites — vNet peering requires non-overlapping address spaces; Azure blocks peering creation when ranges overlap. Peering connects spokes to the hub but doesn't route spoke-to-spoke through it (non-transitive).

Gateway subnet — the gateway subnet hosts active/standby gateway instances plus platform addresses; Microsoft recommends /27 or larger. NAT Gateway provides up to 64k SNAT ports per public IP (up to 16 IPs) at the subnet level — the designed fix for large-scale outbound.

UDR — note: gateway subnets must be named exactly 'GatewaySubnet' and carry no NSG/UDR. UDRs with a default route to the hub firewall/NVA override system routes and force inspection — the classic forced-tunneling/hub inspection design.
Common trap — use a VPN gateway instead of peering.
Common trap — the subnet needs an NSG first.
Common trap — an NSG rule allowing DNS.
Common trap — peer anyway; Azure resolves overlaps automatically.

Private endpoints need private DNS resolution — the privatelink.* zone linked to the VNet maps the service's public FQDN to the private endpoint IP. Without it, clients resolve the public IP and traffic leaves the VNet — silently defeating the purpose.

sections.heading: Connectivity
items: Site-to-site VPN — Site-to-site VPN connects entire on-premises networks to Azure via IPsec from the site's VPN device. Point-to-site VPN gives individual clients (laptops) an encrypted tunnel to the VNet via the VPN gateway — no on-premises VPN hardware needed.
Hybrid connectivity — point-to-site is per-client; ExpressRoute is dedicated private connectivity (overkill for one small branch); peering is Azure-to-Azure only.
Point-to-site VPN — VPN over the internet can't guarantee throughput.

ExpressRoute — global Reach connects ExpressRoute circuits together over Microsoft's backbone — e.g., Azure to another cloud's private interconnect — without traversing the public internet. ExpressRoute has two peering types: private peering (RFC 1918 traffic to your VNet…

Dedicated connectivity — expressRoute provides private, dedicated bandwidth (up to 100 Gbps) with SLA-backed latency/throughput — the choice for bulk, compliance-sensitive, or latency-sensitive traffic.
Common trap — microsoft peering carries VNet traffic.
Common trap — 30 separate site-to-site VPNs with manual routing.
Common trap — increasing the VPN gateway SKU.
Common trap — one giant VNet per branch.

sections.heading: Routing
items: UDR — service endpoints add system routes for the service's public prefixes, which are more specific than a 0.0.0.0/0 UDR — so service traffic should bypass the firewall. Azure system routes send internet-bound traffic directly out; a UDR default route (0.0.0.0/0…

Route override — longest prefix match: the most specific matching route wins, regardless of creation order. Effective routes (portal or Get-AzEffectiveRouteTable) shows the merged result: NIC route table + subnet route table + system routes, with the winning route per prefix.
BGP — BGP exchanges routes dynamically between on-premises and Azure, enabling consistent path selection and automatic failover across redundant connections.
Dynamic routing — nSGs filter traffic but never change its path; routing and filtering are separate mechanisms.
Common trap — service endpoints don't work with UDRs at all.
Common trap — service endpoints require ExpressRoute.
Common trap — the system route wins over UDRs.
Common trap — the VNet address space blade.
Longest prefix match — the most specific matching route wins, regardless of creation order. UDRs override system routes of equal specificity; among UDRs, specificity decides.

sections.heading: Private Access
items: Private Link Service — Private Link Service (the provider side of Private Link) exposes your internal standard load balancer to consumers who create private endpoints in their own VNets — private connectivity with no peering, no public IPs, and consumer-driven approval.
Compliance needs both axes — encrypted AND private.

Private Link Service — secure transfer required enforces HTTPS (encryption in transit); private endpoints with public network access disabled enforce private paths. Service endpoints keep the service's public endpoint (traffic stays on the backbone but the endpoint is still publi…
Provider-side Private Link — each consumer VNet needs its own private DNS zone linked locally — DNS resolution is per-VNet.
Common trap — a bigger private endpoint SKU.

Common trap — keeps the public endpoint, only extends VNet identity.
Common trap — use Azure Front Door instead.

sections.heading: Monitoring
items: Traffic Analytics processes raw NSG flow logs into visual insights — top talkers, application ports, data-center/DC traffic distribution, and malicious-flow flagging — the analysis layer over flow logs.

Connection Monitor — Connection Monitor runs scheduled synthetic probes between endpoints and tracks latency, packet loss, and hop topology over time — the tool for intermittent issues that one-time tests miss.
NSG flow logs — it's the escalation when flow logs and verifiers can't explain the failure. It's the authoritative record of what the NSG did.
Packet capture — network Watcher packet capture records real packets from a VM (or gateway) to blob storage for deep protocol analysis.
Common trap — raw flow logs read manually.
Common trap — measures latency, not rule decisions.
Common trap — reboot the on-premises device first.
Common trap — delete and recreate the gateway immediately.
NSG — NSG flow logs record every flow's allow/deny verdict per rule through the NSG, stored in Log Analytics via Traffic Analytics for KQL querying. It's the authoritative record of what the NSG did.

checklist: Get 7–8 hours of sleep the night before — fatigue destroys recall faster than any topic gap.
Bring valid government-issued photo ID and arrive at the test center 30 minutes early.
Eat a real meal beforehand; bring water and a light snack if the center allows them.
Read every question twice before scanning the answer choices.
Flag uncertain questions and move on — return with fresh eyes at the end.
Eliminate the obviously wrong answers first, then compare the survivors.
Budget your time: answer steadily and keep a 10–15 minute review buffer.
Re-run your weakest-domain drill until mastery is at least 80%.
For VNet Design: restate the 'why' behind each scenario answer in your own words — if you can't explain it, you don't own it.
Redo one Connectivity lab from scratch without looking at the steps.
Recite the key Routing terms from the glossary aloud from memory.
